Agents window: revealing or addressing N feedback comments notifies listeners N times (O(N²) work)

Version: Code - Insiders 1.148.0-insider (d6531fd4b51, 2026-11-24), Linux x64; also on `main` at 00b906dd138.

When several agent-feedback comments are accepted at once, `IAgentFeedbackService.acceptFeedback` is called once per comment, and each call upserts a single item into the backend. Every upsert fires `onDidChangeFeedback` and `onDidChangeNavigation`, and the listeners (editor widgets, overview ruler, decorations, input banners, menus, context keys…) re-read every comment of the session each time. Accepting N comments therefore costs N notifications and about N² item reads.

Two places accept a batch:

- **Review "Reveal" button** (agent feedback review confirmation in chat): runs `agentFeedback.review.accept` with the checked ids, which loops `acceptFeedback(resource, id, { revealToAgent: true })` (`agentFeedbackReviewCommands.ts`).
- **"Address comments" banner** above the chat input: `_acceptComments` loops `acceptFeedback(sessionResource, commentId)` (`sessionInputBannerModel.ts`).

1. In the Agents window, have a session with many review comments, for example PR review comments mirrored as feedback, or comments an agent left with the review tool.
2. Click **Reveal** in the review confirmation, or **Address comments** in the banner.
3. Every comment triggers its own round of change events before the request goes out.

One `onDidChangeFeedback` listener that re-reads `getFeedback`, as the real listeners do. Service with the in-memory backend:

| comments | main: events (feedback + navigation) | main: items read | main: time | batched: events | batched: items read | batched: time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 + 10 | 100 | 0.7 ms | 1 + 1 | 10 | 0.2 ms |
| 100 | 100 + 100 | 10,000 | 16 ms | 1 + 1 | 100 | 0.2 ms |
| 500 | 500 + 500 | 250,000 | 186–465 ms | 1 + 1 | 500 | 3.2 ms |

[image]

This is the same pattern as submitting feedback (`markFeedbackSubmitted`), which also upserts one item at a time.

Accepting a set of comments updates them together and notifies listeners once.

Agents window: submitting N review comments fires N feedback-change events (O(N²) listener work)

In the Agents window, **Submit** sends every pending review comment (agent feedback) to the agent. When the request is accepted, `AgentFeedbackService.markFeedbackSubmitted` marks those comments Submitted, but it calls `backend.upsert` once per comment. Each upsert fires the backend's `onDidChangeItems`, so `_handleBackendChange` fires `onDidChangeFeedback` and `onDidChangeNavigation` once per comment.

About 15 production listeners subscribe to `onDidChangeFeedback`. They include the editor comment widgets, the editor overlay, the overview ruler, the feedback attachment, the Changes view, the session input banners and the PR review seeder and thread resolver. Most of them re-read all of the session's feedback on every event, so submitting N comments costs O(N²) work. For agent-host sessions, the annotations backend makes it worse: each `AnnotationsSet` dispatch notifies the subscription, and `_onAnnotationsChange` re-decodes every annotation in the channel each time.

**Version:** main at 00b906dd138 (and Insiders 1.148.0-insider), Linux x64

The probe submits N comments with a single cheap `onDidChangeFeedback` listener that reads `getFeedback` (unit-test harness, bare `AgentFeedbackService`):

[image]

| comments | events | items read | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 100 | 0.3 ms |
| 100 | 100 | 10,000 | 3.5 ms |
| 500 | 500 | 250,000 | 121 ms |

The real cost is a multiple of this, because every real listener repeats its own work for each event. A unit test that submits 20 comments sees `onDidChangeFeedback` fire 20 times and `onDidChangeNavigation` 20 times.

1. Open a session in the Agents window and add many review comments to its changes, for example on files in the session's worktree.
2. Click **Submit**.
3. All comments move to Submitted in one step, but every feedback listener runs once per comment.

Marking a batch of comments submitted is one change: it should fire `onDidChangeFeedback` and `onDidChangeNavigation` once, and the annotations channel should be reconciled once.

`acceptFeedback` (used by the Accept All command) also upserts one comment per call, so the same per-item fan-out applies there.

Agents window: marking one file reviewed spawns 33 git processes, resolving the same context and working tree 2–3 times

Marking a single file as reviewed in a session's Branch changeset makes the agent host spawn **33 git processes**. Several of them repeat work that was done a few milliseconds earlier in the same action. In one click:

- `merge-base HEAD origin/main` runs 3 times;
- `status` runs 3 times;
- the whole working tree is staged with `add -A` 3 times.

The working tree doesn't change in between. Someone who clicks through the files of a large changeset to review them pays this cost on every click.

Measured on main at 2c3453e4f15 (Linux, git 2.43.0). I drove the agent host server with `--enable-mock-agent` over the protocol, in a worktree session with 20 changed files. A git wrapper counted every spawn and recorded the JS caller of each one.

| Action | git spawns | summed git time | wall time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mark 1 file reviewed | 33 | 233 ms | – |
| Mark 20 files reviewed one by one | **660** | **4,616 ms** | 6,007 ms |

[image]

`ChangesetFilesReviewChanged` is handled in `agentService.ts`. It awaits `IAgentHostReviewService.setReviewState`, then forces `refreshBranchChangeset`, which recomputes the changeset and calls `_computeReviewedInfo` → `getReviewedPaths`:

1. **`_setReviewed`** (15 spawns):
   - `_resolveContext` resolves the session refs and the baseline: `rev-parse` ×3, `show-ref`, `merge-base`.
   - `captureWorkingTreeAsTree`: `status`, `rev-parse`, `add -A`, `write-tree`.
   - `overlayPathIntoTree`: `read-tree`, `ls-tree`, `update-index`, `write-tree`.
   - `commit-tree`, `update-ref`.
2. **Forced Branch refresh** (7 spawns):
   - the fingerprint resolves the merge base again: `show-ref`, `rev-parse HEAD`, `status`, `merge-base`;
   - the branch diff stages the working tree again: `read-tree HEAD`, `add -A`, `diff --cached`.
3. **`getReviewedPaths`** (11 spawns):
   - `_resolveContext` again, with the same result as step 1;
   - `captureWorkingTreeAsTree` again, with the same tree as step 1;
   - `diff --name-only` ×2.

One review click should resolve the session's context and capture the working tree once. For example:

- `setReviewState` could return the reviewed paths it can compute from the tree it just wrote;
- or the review service could keep the resolved context and the captured tree for the `getReviewedPaths` call of the refresh that follows;
- the fingerprint could reuse the merge base it resolved.

That would remove roughly 12–15 of the 33 spawns per click.

Agents window: Merge, Commit and Sync wait for the Git state refresh's 5 s cooldown before returning

In the Agents window, the changeset actions **Merge**, **Commit** and **Sync** stay busy at least 5 seconds longer than the git work they do. When a session's Branch changeset is merged, the button keeps spinning for about 6 s although git finished in under 1 s.

I drove the agent host (`--enable-mock-agent`) over the agent-host protocol with 3 worktree sessions and a logging git wrapper, and invoked the changeset operations the way the Changes view does.

| Changeset action | git spawns | git time | Action time (invoke → result) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Merge, session Branch changeset | 45 | 885 ms | **5,818 ms** |
| Discard 1 file, Uncommitted changeset | 16 | 110 ms | 15 ms |
| Discard 5 files one by one | 32 | 221 ms | 18 ms |

Merge spends about 4.9 s doing nothing.

After the action, each of these handlers awaits a forced Git state refresh:

- `AgentHostMergeOperationHandler`: `await this._onGitStateChanged(...)` in its `finally`
- `AgentHostCommitOperationHandler`: `await this._onCommitted(...)`
- `AgentHostSyncOperationHandler`: `await this._onSynced(...)`

The refresh goes through `AgentHostChangesetOperationService._refreshGitState`, which forces `refreshSessionGitState` on the source and the session with `Promise.all`. `AgentHostGitStateService._refreshSessionGitState` queues the read in a `ThrottlerByKey`, and the task ends with:

```
// Throttle git state refreshes to avoid excessive git operations
await timeout(5_000);
```

`Throttler.queue` only resolves its callers when the task has finished, which is after that 5 s sleep. Every awaited refresh therefore costs the caller at least 5 s, even though the new Git state was read and published within milliseconds. Discard calls the same refresh with `void`, which is why it returns in 15 ms.

The cooldown itself is useful: it keeps bursts of refreshes from running git back to back. Only the caller's wait is the problem.

An awaited refresh resolves once it has read and published the Git state. The next refresh of the same session still waits out the cooldown, as it does today.

The BEFORE/AFTER image shows a fake-timer unit test. It counts how many 5 s pauses an awaited refresh makes its caller wait (main: 1 for the first refresh and 2 for a second one queued behind it; expected: 0 and 1). It also shows the Merge timing on main and with a fix that releases callers once the state is published: **5,818 ms → 296 ms**, with the same git work.

Agent host Branch Changes recompute runs show-ref, merge-base and status twice

When a session's Branch Changes may have changed, `AgentHostChangesetService` does two things in a row:

1. It calls `getBranchDiffFingerprint`, which runs `show-ref --verify refs/remotes/origin/<base>`, `merge-base HEAD <base>`, `rev-parse HEAD` and `status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all`.
2. When the fingerprint changed, it immediately calls `computeSessionFileDiffs`, which runs the **same** `show-ref`, `merge-base` and `status` again before `read-tree`, `add -A` and `diff --cached`.

So every recompute spends 3 extra git spawns. One of them is a full `status` with untracked files, the most expensive read in a large worktree.

Version: Code - Insiders 1.148.0-insider / main 7df2c7e8193, Linux x64, git 2.43.0

I drove the real agent host (`--enable-mock-agent`) over the Agent Host Protocol and counted git spawns with a logging `git` wrapper. The data was fake: 10 sessions × 6 chats, a 3,000-file repository, and 60 modified plus 20 untracked files per session.

- At 6,000 turns, the turns phase ran 14,453 `show-ref`, 11,689 `merge-base` and 19,796 `status`. About 3,900 Branch recomputes each repeated 3 of them: about **11,700 git spawns**.
- An A/B at 600 turns, origin/main against a build that reuses the fingerprint's values (combined with two related fixes): `status` went from 2,038 to 1,637, `show-ref` from 1,575 to 710, and `merge-base` from 1,252 to 437.

[image]

`computeSessionFileDiffs` reuses the merge base and status output that the fingerprint just recorded, and produces the same diffs.

Related: #350103 (open) changes how the merge base is resolved and removes the `show-ref`; the duplicated `merge-base` and `status` remain. Also related: #349692 (closed).

Agent host review state resolves the branch baseline even when nothing was reviewed

On every Branch Changes recompute, `AgentHostReviewService._getReviewedPaths` calls `_resolveContext`. That method first resolves the branch baseline (`resolveBranchBaselineCommit`: `show-ref` and `merge-base`, then `rev-parse <baseline>^{tree}`), and only then looks up the session's reviewed ref. When no file was ever marked as reviewed, the common case, the result is an empty set, and the 3 baseline spawns were wasted.

Version: Code - Insiders 1.148.0-insider / main 7df2c7e8193, Linux x64, git 2.43.0

I drove the real agent host (`--enable-mock-agent`) over the Agent Host Protocol and counted git spawns with a logging `git` wrapper. The data was fake: 10 sessions × 6 chats × 100 turns, with nothing marked reviewed.

- At 6,000 turns, about 3,900 Branch recomputes × 3 = about **11,700 git spawns** for an empty result.
- An A/B at 600 turns, origin/main against a build that checks the reviewed ref first (combined with two related fixes): `show-ref` went from 1,575 to 710 and `merge-base` from 1,252 to 437. This change and the Branch Changes fingerprint reuse each remove one of each per recompute.

[image]

Look up the reviewed ref first, including the legacy folder-owned ref, and skip resolving the baseline when there is none. The legacy migration keeps working.

Agent host checkpoint resolves the baseline and parent refs twice every turn

Each agent turn, `AgentHostCheckpointService` runs `git rev-parse --verify` 4 times where 2 are enough:

- Turn start calls `getBaselineCheckpoint`, which resolves `refs/agents/<session>/checkpoints/turn/0` and creates the baseline when it is missing.
- Turn end calls `getBaselineCheckpoint` again for the same ref, although the start just found or created it.
- `_getRepositoryParentRef` resolves the previous turn's ref to choose it, and the caller then resolves the same ref again to get its commit.

Version: Code - Insiders 1.148.0-insider / main 7df2c7e8193, Linux x64, git 2.43.0

I drove the real agent host (`--enable-mock-agent`) over the Agent Host Protocol and counted git spawns with a logging `git` wrapper. The data was fake: 10 sessions, each with 6 chats on their own worktree, and a 3,000-file repository. Every turn edited files.

- At 10 sessions × 6 chats × 100 turns = 6,000 turns, the turns phase ran 47,619 `rev-parse --verify`. Four of them per turn come from the checkpoint service, and 2 of those are redundant: about **12,000 git spawns**.
- An A/B at 600 turns, origin/main against a build that reuses the resolved refs (combined with two related fixes): `rev-parse --verify` went from 4,782 to 3,252, and this change accounts for 2 per turn, about 1,200.

[image]

Turn end reuses the baseline that turn start found or created, and the parent lookup returns the commit it resolved, so each ref is resolved once per turn.

Related: #349692 (closed), which would have coalesced identical in-flight git reads behind a setting.

Remote terminal layout is never persisted, so terminals are not restored after the remote server restarts

Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes (core code path, read in source; the repro needs only the WSL extension to open the remote window)

- VS Code Version: 1.147.0 (8a14f0cc1b)
- OS Version: Windows 11 (10.0.26300), remote WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04

With `terminal.integrated.persistentSessionReviveProcess: onExitAndWindowClose`, terminals in a remote window are not restored once the remote server restarts (reboot, `wsl --shutdown`, server update). The processes are revived, but no tabs appear.

Cause: `RemoteTerminalBackend.setTerminalLayoutInfo` only forwards the layout to the pty host, which keeps it in memory (`_workspaceLayoutInfos`). Unlike `LocalTerminalBackend`, it never stores `TerminalStorageKeys.TerminalLayoutInfo`:

- Local, stores it: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/f782cb3bcee0c64f205f4d575135b4fe92a8ee8a/src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminal/electron-browser/localTerminalBackend.ts#L318-L328
- Remote, doesn't: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/f782cb3bcee0c64f205f4d575135b4fe92a8ee8a/src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminal/browser/remoteTerminalBackend.ts#L316-L322

`RemoteTerminalBackend.getTerminalLayoutInfo` already reads that key after reviving `TerminalBufferState` ([L339-L357](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/f782cb3bcee0c64f205f4d575135b4fe92a8ee8a/src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminal/browser/remoteTerminalBackend.ts#L339-L357)), but nothing writes it. A fresh pty host returns no layout, so the revived processes are never attached: `ptyhost.log` shows `Revived process, old id … -> new id …` with no `Expanding terminal instance` / `Persistent process reconnection` after it, and the window opens with no terminals.

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Set `"terminal.integrated.persistentSessionReviveProcess": "onExitAndWindowClose"`.
2. Open a folder in WSL, open two terminals and type in each.
3. Close the window, run `wsl --shutdown` from Windows, reopen the folder.
4. No terminals appear. `~/.vscode-server/data/logs/<start>/ptyhost.log` shows the processes revived.

Expected: the remote backend stores the layout in workspace storage as the local backend does, so terminals are restored after a server restart.

Canvas activation can be remembered for the wrong folder location after overlapping or failed switches

Switching Folder Location should remember whether a canvas was the active tab independently for each location. Returning to a location should restore its previous selection, even if another location switch was requested while editors were still being restored or a restore attempt failed.

The ordinary round trip is addressed by #350127. Two edge cases remain where a canvas's activation state can be recorded against the wrong location, causing a canvas to return as a background tab when it should be active, or vice versa.

1. **Another location change while restoration is pending:** Start at location A with a canvas open. Switch to B, then request C before B's editor working set finishes applying. The canvas service can treat C as the editor area's owner while the editor area still belongs to B. The next switch can then save the canvas's active state under the wrong location.
2. **Restore fails before closing the canvas:** Start at A and switch to B when B's stored editor working set cannot be applied, for example because its saved working-set state is missing. The first apply fails without closing the canvas. The fallback that empties the editor area can then record A's canvas activation as B's, overwriting B's previously remembered state.

Use one source of truth for the location whose editors are being shown. `FolderLocationWorkingSets` already captures the location being left and the target being entered, and advances its owner only after applying a working set succeeds. Expose that switch context through a shared contract consumed by the canvas service, rather than having the canvas service infer ownership from the current workspace folder and generic working-set completion events.

Add regression tests for both sequences, including a return to a location whose remembered canvas activation differs from the outgoing location. Preserve the existing ordinary round-trip and hidden-chat behavior.

Agents window: session lookups rebuild and scan every session on each agent-host notification

In the Agents window, every agent-host session notification makes consumers call `SessionsManagementService.getSession(resource)`. Each call rebuilds the full session list from every provider (`getAllSessions`) and scans it linearly. With a few hundred sessions this keeps the renderer main thread busy: in a captured trace most of the window's main-thread time went to notification handling, and `getSession`/`getAllSessions` were the top costs.

The agent-host provider's `getAllSessions` makes it worse: for every saved Claude/Codex session it re-reads two settings (`configurationService.inspect`) to decide whether the agent is policy-unavailable, although the answer is the same for every session of that agent.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Have several hundred agent sessions (Copilot, Claude, Codex) in the Agents window.
2. Use the window while sessions are active, so agent-host notifications arrive.
3. Record a performance trace: `getSession` and `getAllSessions` dominate the main thread.

Expected: looking up a session by resource does not enumerate every session, and the settings are read once per agent per listing.

Permission prompts from nested parallel subagents never appear, so the session blocks indefinitely (Copilot harness)

Summary
A custom agent workflow delegates to a coordinator subagent. The coordinator starts 3–4 reviewer subagents in parallel using the task tool. When several reviewers request approval for terminal commands, some of the prompts are never shown anywhere in the UI. Those reviewers wait forever, the coordinator waits on them, and the whole session hangs. The only recovery is to restart VS Code.

This started after updating VS Code, when the workflow moved from the Local harness to the Copilot harness. It had worked reliably for months on the Local harness.

Occurs in the editor's Chat view using the Copilot harness (Agent Host); not using the Agents window.

Setup

Main chat agent → coordinator subagent (custom agent) → 4 reviewer subagents (custom agents), started in parallel.
The reviewers run shell commands, including multi-line PowerShell here-strings piped into python - (only "Allow Once" is offered for these).
Steps to reproduce

In a Copilot harness chat with Manual permissions, invoke a custom agent that delegates to a subagent.
Have that subagent start 3–4 subagents in parallel, each of which runs commands that need approval.
Approve prompts as they appear.
Expected
Every pending approval prompt is shown, in the main chat and/or the subagent's view, so the user can approve or skip it.

Actual

The first few prompts appear in the main chat's subagent status area and are approved.
Prompts raised soon afterwards by other reviewers never appear in the main chat, the "N subagents running" list, or the individual subagent tabs. Opening a stuck subagent's tab shows its last message and no approval control.
The session log shows each request as permission.requested with no matching permission.completed.
No timeout or error occurs. The session stays at "4 subagents running" indefinitely.
Example timeline (11/24, local time)

8:26: coordinator starts 4 reviewers in parallel.
8:31:24 and 8:31:42: two reviewer prompts appear and are approved.
8:35:16, 8:35:44, 8:39:22: three more reviewer prompts are raised. None are ever displayed.
8:39: the one reviewer that needed no further approval completes.
Over 50 minutes later: still "4 subagents running" (the coordinator plus the 3 blocked reviewers). No way to approve.
Frequency
Reproduced in at least 4 sessions between 11/12 and 11/24. Blocked reviewers waited up to about 25 hours, until VS Code was restarted.

Additional notes

Approval prompts from the first-level subagent (the coordinator) appear reliably.
The problem only occurs with second-level subagents running in parallel.

Expose the sash double-click sizing of the Side Bar (and Panel) as a command that can be bound to a key

Double-clicking the sash between the Primary Side Bar and the editor area resizes the Side Bar so its contents fit (e.g. long file names in the Explorer are no longer truncated). This is very handy, but today it is **mouse-only**: there is no command that does the same thing, so it can't be bound to a keyboard shortcut or used in `runCommands` sequences.

Schematic example:

[image]

Add a command (name is just a suggestion), e.g.:

- `workbench.action.resetSideBarSize` – does exactly what double-clicking the Primary Side Bar sash does

Ideally with equivalents for the other parts that have the same double-click behavior:

- `workbench.action.resetAuxiliaryBarSize` (Secondary Side Bar)
- `workbench.action.resetPanelSize` (Panel)

No default keybinding is needed; users could bind it themselves:

```
{ "key": "ctrl+alt+0", "command": "workbench.action.resetSideBarSize" }
```

- Keyboard-centric users currently have to reach for the mouse and hit a 4px sash precisely.
- The right width depends on the content (file names, folder depth, which view is shown), so a fixed width is not a substitute.
- Accessibility: the action is currently only available through a precise double-click gesture.

- `workbench.action.increaseViewWidth` / `decreaseViewWidth`: they only resize in fixed steps and don't take the content into account.
- Chaining them with `runCommands` (shrink to minimum, then grow N steps) gives a fixed width, not a content-based one.
- Extensions can't do this, since they have no access to the workbench layout/DOM.

Remote agent host pins the launching connection's REMOTE_CONTAINERS_IPC/SSH_AUTH_SOCK; agent git and SSH auth fail once it ends

Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: No. It needs a remote whose resolver supplies a per-connection environment (Dev Containers here); the defect is in core, see "Cause".

- VS Code Version: 1.147.0 (8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5); the code involved is unchanged on `main` (00b906dd)
- OS Version: macOS (Apple Silicon); remote: Dev Containers on Podman, Ubuntu 24.04 arm64
- Agent: Copilot sessions in the server-owned agent host (lazy launch)

Follow-up to #340566, which forwards the resolver's `extensionHostEnv` to the server-owned agent host and keeps it for crash restarts.

The agent host is one process per server, shared by all windows, and its environment is the `extensionHostEnv` of the connection that launched it. Dev Containers puts per-connection sockets in that map: `REMOTE_CONTAINERS_IPC` for git credentials, and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. Each new Dev Containers connection (after a window reload, for example) gets new sockets, but the agent host keeps the first ones: later connects don't update them, and a crash relaunch reuses them. Everything it spawns inherits them: the Copilot runtime, tool shells, MCP servers. Once the launching connection's forwarding stops answering, agent sessions in every window lose git credentials and the SSH agent, while the windows' terminals and extension hosts keep working. Git then falls back to `GIT_ASKPASS`, and the agent asks the user for a GitHub username and password.

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Open a folder in a dev container (window A) with git credential forwarding working. The server log shows `[AgentHostChannel] Renderer … requested connect to upstream`, then `ServerAgentHostManager: agent host started`.
2. Reload window A, or open a second window on the same container. It gets a new Dev Containers connection with new sockets.
3. In a new integrated terminal, `echo $REMOTE_CONTAINERS_IPC $SSH_AUTH_SOCK` prints that window's current sockets.
4. Ask the agent in that window to run the same command: it prints the sockets of window A's connection from step 1.
5. Once that connection's forwarding no longer answers (here, by the next day, after several window reconnects), ask the agent to run `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<private-repo>`. The Dev Containers credential helper returns nothing and git asks for a username and password through `GIT_ASKPASS`. The same command in a terminal succeeds.

Expected: commands run by an agent session use live forwarding: that of the session's window, as its terminals and extension host do, or at least that of a connected window.

Two windows on one container, 2026-11-24 (UTC). For each process, `REMOTE_CONTAINERS_IPC` and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` name the same connection. I ran the Dev Containers helper (`node /tmp/vscode-remote-containers-<id>.js git-credential-helper get` with `protocol=https`, `host=github.com`) with the process's `REMOTE_CONTAINERS_IPC`, and `ssh-add -l` with its `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`:

| Process | Connection | git credential | `ssh-add -l` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agent host, relaunched 10:07:51, and the Copilot runtime it started at 10:10:52 | `76d1d3e2…`, created 2026-11-23 11:05:21 with the server | none (helper exits 255) | exit 1, no identities |
| Window 1 extension host, started 10:10:51 | `0b15c0f7…` | username and password | exit 0 |
| Window 2 extension host, started 10:41:58 | `3f002177…` | username and password | exit 0 |
| Integrated terminal shells | `31018b1e…`, `6f77ae8a…`, `dcce35f6…` | username and password | exit 0 |

Server log (`remoteagent.log`):

```
2026-11-24 10:07:50.653 [error] ServerAgentHostManager: agent host terminated unexpectedly with code null
2026-11-24 10:07:51.891 [info] ServerAgentHostManager: agent host started
2026-11-24 10:10:44.334 [info] [AgentHostChannel] Renderer ctx=[object Object] requested connect to upstream
2026-11-24 10:10:51.650 [info] [127.0.0.1][9cbbbc79][ExtensionHostConnection] <423802> Launched Extension Host Process.
2026-11-24 10:41:38.186 [info] [AgentHostChannel] Renderer ctx=[object Object] requested connect to upstream
2026-11-24 10:41:58.879 [info] [127.0.0.1][63190e44][ExtensionHostConnection] <449326> Launched Extension Host Process.
```

The 10:07:51 relaunch got the environment of the connection that started the server 23 hours earlier. Since that first launch, the log had recorded 6 new management connections and 145 `requested connect to upstream` calls. Neither window connect after the relaunch changed the running process. The relaunched agent host registered itself in `~/.config/Code/agent-host/local-endpoint/entries/` (`"type": "standalone"`, `"pid": 421047`).

1. Each renderer connect sends its window's current `extensionHostEnv`:
   https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5/src/vs/workbench/services/agentHost/browser/editorRemoteAgentHostServiceClient.ts#L134-L145
2. The lazy launch callback ignores that environment when it finds a registered agent host, and the server's own agent host is registered once it runs. Only the connect that launches it reaches `setEnvironment`:
   https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5/src/vs/server/node/serverServices.ts#L322-L348
3. The starter keeps that snapshot and merges it into every later launch (L162), including the relaunch after an unexpected exit:
   https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5/src/vs/platform/agentHost/node/nodeAgentHostStarter.ts#L83-L86
   https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5/src/vs/server/node/serverAgentHostManager.ts#L305-L310

Without the registry check, a new snapshot would still only reach the next launch, because `ensureStarted()` returns the running process.

- Or keep a process-wide snapshot, but refresh it on every connect, including when the registered endpoint is the server's own agent host. Apply it to processes spawned afterwards, and drop it when its connection is removed.

With the sandbox enabled, the MCP server fails with "'npx' is not recognized as an internal or external command". The sandbox redirects LOCALAPPDATA to the sandbox container, and VOLTA_HOME is not set. Volta resolves its tool directory from LOCALAPPDATA, so its shims can't find the installed Node/npm. Workaround: set VOLTA_HOME=%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Volta as a user environment variable and allow read/write access to that folder in the sandbox paths. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes — the rebind happens in the built-in agent host (`vs/platform/agentHost`), not in a third-party extension. The severe stall additionally requires third-party skill plugins to be enabled.

- VS Code Version: 1.147.0 (commit `8a14f0cc1b`, 2026-11-17)
- OS Version: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26300

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Open a new agent-host chat window with third-party skill plugins enabled (superpowers, karpathy).
2. Send a first message. It completes normally (`timeToFirstProgress` ≈ 9 s).
3. Wait for the SDK process to go idle. The plugin cache's `.in_use/<pid>` marker is removed and `agenthost.log` records `File Watcher: watched path got deleted`.
4. Send a second message in the same chat.

Actual:

`agenthost.log` shows `rebinding before turn ... for changed client customizations`, followed by **two** `rebuild isResume=true` entries within ~0.7 s:

```
<t+0.00s> rebinding before turn <request-id> for changed client customizations
<t+0.01s> rebuild isResume=true agent=(none)
<t+0.20s> _processMessages crashed: Error: Claude SDK stream ended without a result message
<t+0.66s> rebuild isResume=true agent=(none)
```

The model finishes the turn normally: the transcript shows the assistant's final message at `<t+2m09s>`.

The host does not forward the result. `AgentHostFirstProgress` is only recorded at `<t+4m58s>` (`timeToFirstProgress=298149`).

Sending another message while the turn is stalled (`<t+4m49s>`) flushes the queue; the result appears ~5 s later.

A second severe occurrence shows the same pattern: two rebuilds and `timeToFirstProgress=207981`.

Expected:

- The host should not treat volatile plugin-cache state as a client-customization change.
- If a rebind is required, the rebuilt pipeline should forward the model's output without waiting for another user message.

Additional reproducible finding:

With all plugins disabled and the MCP config removed, `rebinding before turn` still occurs on many turns (13 times in one session), but each turn performs only **one** `rebuild isResume=true`, and `timeToFirstProgress` drops to 5–11 s. The 3–5 min stall no longer reproduces.

This isolates the stall to the double-rebuild path: the first rebuild is triggered by the plugin-cache change; the second appears to be triggered by the plugin `load.kind` transition from `loading` to `loaded`.

Workaround:

- Send a short message while the turn is stalled; the queued result is flushed.
- Disabling all third-party plugins avoids the stall, but the rebind still occurs.

When I pick a local branch (`master`) as the base branch for an Agents session, the **Changes** view compares the session against `origin/master` instead. If local `master` has commits that haven't been pushed, all of them show up as changes made by the session.

1. In a repo with an `origin` remote, commit something to local `master` and don't push it, so `master` is ahead of `origin/master`.
2. In the Agents window, start a worktree session and choose `master` as the base branch. The session branch's reflog shows `branch: Created from master`, and `get_current_session` reports `baseBranch: "master"`.
3. Make any change in the session.
4. Open **Changes**.

The Changes view includes everything from the unpushed `master` commit in addition to the session's changes. It shows 10 files when `git diff master` shows 6.

The Changes view should compare against the base branch I picked: `merge-base HEAD master`. I chose a local branch on purpose. That's what I'd like to compare against.

[`_resolveBranchMergeBaseCommit`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/platform/agentHost/node/agentHostGitService.ts) replaces the base with its remote-tracking ref whenever one exists:

```
const resolvedBase = await this._resolveRemoteTrackingBranch(repositoryRoot, baseBranch) ?? baseBranch;
mergeBaseCommit = (await this._runGit(repositoryRoot, ['merge-base', 'HEAD', resolvedBase]))?.trim();
```

The doc comment says this is so that "branch changes match a PR-style comparison even if the local base branch is stale". That assumption only works when the local base is *behind* its remote. When the local base is *ahead*, which is normal if you use local branches or haven't pushed yet, the swap is wrong: it diffs against a commit the session branch never started from.

The user can't change this. The built-in Git extension's `branch.<name>.vscode-merge-base` setting also rejects local branches (`getBranchBase()` in `extensions/git/src/repository.ts` only accepts a remote branch) and maps them to their upstream. So setting it to `master` gets silently rewritten to `origin/master`.

Use the base branch the user selected. Some options:

- If the local base contains the remote-tracking ref (`merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<base> <base>`), use the local base. It is at least as current and is what the branch was created from.
- Or diff against the branch's creation point from the reflog (`branch: Created from <base>`).
- At minimum, let the user choose or override the comparison base in the Changes view (also asked for in #321941 and #337971).

Related: #321941, #337971, #347855, #341805.

Copilot Chat sessions that belong to a project/workspace folder are effectively bound to the folder's absolute path. After moving the project folder, those project sessions are no longer shown. Moving the folder back to its original path restores them.

This is not file loss: the session data still exists. It is a session identity and access problem. Copying the files, reopening the workspace, restarting VS Code, and manually rewriting the local Copilot storage did not durably restore access; only restoring the old path worked.

This is primarily a bug report: a normal folder move makes existing project sessions inaccessible. The migration and re-association ideas below are proposed fixes/enhancements.

The same path-binding pattern was also observed in a third-party chat extension: in this project, the Claude Code extension's history was tied to the old workspace path and could be continued only after a manual JSONL migration and path rewrite. Claude Code is only one observed example. Any AI chat extension that keys project-scoped history to an absolute path—for example Gemini, Grok, or future assistants—is likely to fail the same way. A stable workspace identity and migration contract from VS Code would let all first- and third-party chat extensions handle folder moves consistently, instead of fixing one extension at a time.

Sandbox profiles: concurrent windows can lose a host's last-known profile assignment

Follow-up to #350008 (backport: #350019). Refs #349807.

All windows on a machine share the saved list of each remote host's last-known sandbox profile (`chat.sandboxProfileAssignments.v1`, `APPLICATION_SHARED`). `rememberSandboxProfileAssignment` in `src/vs/platform/agentHost/common/sandboxProfiles.ts` reads the whole list from the window's cached storage, changes one entry and writes the whole list back.

Each window's cache only sees other windows' writes after they propagate. When two windows record different hosts before either sees the other's write, the second write replaces the list and drops the other host's entry.

1. Open two windows on the same machine that show different remote hosts in Remote Environments, for example host A in window 1 and host B in window 2, each with a sandbox profile assigned.
2. Have both windows record their host's assignment at about the same time, before shared storage propagates between them (for example, both connect at once).
3. Disconnect the host whose entry was written first.

The disconnected host shows its last-known sandbox profile, disabled, and that profile can't be deleted in Manage Sandbox Profiles.

The host's entry is gone, so:
- the Sandbox Profile column shows **Default** for the disconnected host, which is the original #349807 symptom;
- the profile is no longer protected from deletion.

It corrects itself the next time a window shows that host connected.

Update the list with `IStorageService.compareAndSwapApplicationSharedValue`, retrying against the current value, so concurrent updates to different hosts merge instead of overwriting each other. Add a test with two independent window caches and delayed propagation.

Feedback from r/vscode: "Agent window doesn't display chat instances for sessions connected in a dev container."

Since 1.147 (#346859), a Dev Container editor window and the Agents window share the agent host in the container, so the Agents window lists the editor window's chats while it's connected to that container. But the Agents window only knows about containers it has started a session in itself, and doesn't reconnect to those on its own, so people who work in a **Reopen in Container** window don't see their chats there.

Steps:

1. Open a folder with **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**, and start a chat in the Chat view with the Copilot harness.
2. Open the Agents window. The chat isn't listed.
3. In the editor window, run **Open in Agents Window** from the Chat view's **...** menu. The Agents window selects the container's source folder with **Use Dev Container** in a new chat, instead of opening the chat from step 1 (also seen with **Open in Agents** in #349395).
4. Send a message in that new chat. Once the Agents window has connected to the container, it lists the chat from step 1 as well.

Why, in the code:

- The Agents window has a sessions provider for a container only after connecting to it itself: it stores the container once that connection publishes a session ([devContainerAgentHostService.ts](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/4b879e3a6e640e05dcfe9fd22434b3023fd4e782/src/vs/workbench/contrib/sessions/providers/remoteAgentHost/browser/devContainerAgentHostService.ts#L559-L566)). So for a container it has used before, chats started in the editor window since then are missing until something reconnects it.
- `resolveAndOpenRemoteSession` returns `'unsupported'` for Dev Container windows, so **Open in Agents Window** falls back to the source folder ([chat.contribution.ts](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/4b879e3a6e640e05dcfe9fd22434b3023fd4e782/src/vs/sessions/contrib/chat/electron-browser/chat.contribution.ts#L420-L426)). - **Open in Agents Window** in a Dev Container window opens its chat in the Agents window, as it does for SSH, WSL and tunnel windows.

Editor window: feed the agent-host session list of ChatSessionsService from the sessions provider (one source of truth)

With the new sessions list on (`chat.viewSessions.sessionsList.enabled`), a local editor window keeps two copies of the agent-host session list:

1. The new list, backed by `BaseAgentHostSessionsProvider`, which batches changes and updates one session at a time.
2. A second copy for `IChatSessionsService`: `AgentHostSessionListStore` (its own subscription to the host's root notifications and its own cache of every session's summary) plus `AgentHostSessionListController`, which converts those summaries into `IChatSessionItem`s. `AgentSessionsModel`, the chat context picker, chat input completions, the session link opener and the in-progress count read this copy.

The Agents window has no second copy: `AgentHostSessionListContribution` returns early there. So the per-session filtering of the provider does not apply to the readers of `IChatSessionsService` in the editor window, and their cost follows the host's `root/sessionSummaryChanged` rate (see #349477 and #349478 for the batching fix that bounded it).

Proposal: when the new list is on in a local editor window, the controller's item list and change feed come from the sessions provider (`ISession`s and `onDidChangeSessions`) instead of the store, while the controller keeps owning the actions (create, delete, archive, read, moved-chat retargeting, working-directory resolution). The new list off keeps today's path.

Open questions:
- There is no `ISession` to `IChatSessionItem` mapping yet; it must be written and kept equivalent to the store-based one (label, status, archived, read, activity, timing, changes, metadata such as branch, working directory, project and adoptable, and children from chats).
- Provider lifetime: `IEditorWindowSessionsRuntime` holds the sessions providers of an editor window only while the Chat view or the chat part is visible. The readers of `IChatSessionsService` (in-progress count, link opener, context picker) must keep working while they are hidden. Either the controller falls back to the store when the providers are not held (two sources again, and the switch must not emit false deltas), or the window holds the providers for as long as the new list is on.
- The store does not become unused: the controller's actions and the moved-chat catalog read it, and `agentHostWorktreeLocations` creates its own store.

Folder doesn't follow a chat isolated in a multi-chat session after the agent host restarts

In an editor window with `chat.editorWindow.enableWorktree` on, the window's folder follows the shown chat into the worktree that chat works in. When one chat of a session with several chats is isolated into a new worktree (for example with the agent's `isolate_session` tool), the folder follows it and the worktree is listed under Folder Location > Worktrees. This relies on the session summary's `vscode.isolatedChatWorktrees` `_meta` entry, which the agent host publishes as it isolates or restores such a chat.

After the agent host restarts, this no longer works for such a chat until the session's marker reaches the window again:

Steps:
1. In a folder window with `chat.editorWindow.enableWorktree` on, start an agent host chat, add a second chat to its session, and isolate the first chat into a new worktree. The folder follows it.
2. Quit and relaunch VS Code, so that the agent host restarts.
3. Open the isolated chat again.

Expected: the folder moves to that chat's worktree, and the worktree is listed under Folder Location > Worktrees.
Actual: the folder stays where it is, and the worktree is not listed.

Cause: the session list the window holds is the agent host catalog's summary, which the host rebuilds from persisted session values after a restart. The `vscode.isolatedChatWorktrees` marker is published only on the live session state and isn't persisted, so the catalog summary doesn't carry it, and the provider doesn't offer the worktree.

Proposed fix: persist the marker as a central session value (agentHostSessionStateMirror) and project it into the catalog summary on listing, with restart and older-build coverage.

Agents window: send_remote_message stops for good after 50 sends per window lifetime; only a window reload resets it

The [`send_remote_message` tool](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/336682) starts failing with `Remote message limit reached (50 requests per window).` after a window has sent 50 messages in total. The count never decreases, so the cap works as a lifetime budget, not a rate limit. Every agent session in the window shares that budget. Agents can't reload the window, so long-running multi-host coordination stops until a person notices and runs **Developer: Reload Window**.

1. In VS Code 1.147.0 (commit `8a14f0cc1b08`), open the Agents window with two or more agent hosts (Remote-SSH agent hosts in our case) and `chat.remoteSessions.tools.enabled` on.
2. From any agent sessions in that window, call `send_remote_message` 50 times. The calls can be spread over hours and across sessions, and some of them can fail (for example, an unavailable host).
3. The 51st call, from any session, fails with `Remote message limit reached (50 requests per window).`
4. Run **Developer: Reload Window**. Sends work again.

Observed 2026-11-20 on macOS with two Linux agent hosts: two coordination messages failed unsent after a day of normal multi-host traffic, and delivery resumed after a reload. From the source (not tested separately), waiting, closing sessions or toggling `chat.remoteSessions.tools.enabled` does not reset the count, because the router holding it is created once per window and never cleared.

[`remoteSessionMessageRouter.ts`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/ef689d2482cc643608fd4bb098e4b8f43524ebce/src/vs/sessions/contrib/remoteSessions/browser/remoteSessionMessageRouter.ts#L32) (main `ef689d24`; the cap logic is unchanged since 3bc56b58fe, #336690):

- `const maxRemoteMessages = 50;` (L32) is a constant with no setting.
- `RemoteSessionMessageRouter.requests` (L74) is a `Map` keyed by `[source chat, tool call id]`. It exists to make a retried tool call idempotent: the same call with the same input returns the original promise. `send()` (L91–108) rejects new calls once `requests.size >= maxRemoteMessages`.
- Entries are only added (`set`, L106) and never deleted. `SendRemoteMessageTool` creates the router once, and `workbench.contrib.remoteSessionTools` creates that tool once per window, so the map only grows.
- The entry is added before the send resolves. Sends that fail during routing (unknown target, host offline) count against the cap.
- The idempotency cache and the abuse limit are therefore the same structure. Retries need only recent or in-flight entries, but the limit counts everything ever sent.

The cap should protect against a runaway loop without ending legitimate long-lived coordination. Any of the following would do:

1. **Bound the rate, not the lifetime.** For example, count sends in a sliding window (N per M minutes) and evict idempotency entries after they settle plus a retry TTL.
2. **Don't count failed sends**, or refund them when routing fails before anything is delivered.
3. **Scope the budget per source session** (perhaps with a larger per-window ceiling), so one chatty session can't block every other session in the window.
4. **Make it configurable** (e.g. `chat.remoteSessions.tools.maxMessages`), and put the remaining budget and the reset condition in the error text, e.g. "Reload the window to reset". Today the message doesn't say how to recover.
5. Optionally, provide a command that resets the budget, since a full reload interrupts everything else running in the window.

A person runs **Developer: Reload Window** in the Agents window. Agents have no tool to do this. Our agent guidance now tells them to budget sends, and when they hit the error, to report BLOCKED and ask the user to reload.

VS Code Server has grown 4x since 1.100, mostly from two Copilot runtimes

The Linux x64 VS Code Server download grew from 58 MiB in 1.100 to 233 MiB in 1.147. Unpacked, 1.147 takes 684 MiB on disk, and 264 MiB of that is two different builds of the Copilot runtime.

This came up as user feedback on r/vscode: on machines shared by several developers, `/home` filled up because of the VS Code Server, and people avoid Remote-SSH because of it.

Size of `vscode-server-linux-x64.tar.gz` from `https://update.code.visualstudio.com/<version>/server-linux-x64/stable`:

| Version | Download |
|---|---|
| 1.100.0 | 58 MiB |
| 1.114.0 | 86 MiB |
| 1.116.0 | 108 MiB |
| 1.126.0 | 163 MiB |
| 1.132.0 | 217 MiB |
| 1.147.0 | 233 MiB |

1.147.0, unpacked:

| Folder | Size | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `node_modules/@github/copilot-sdk-linux-x64` | 192 MiB | The agent host's Copilot SDK (`@microsoft/copilot-sdk-*` on `main`). 157 MiB of it is `prebuilds/linux-x64/runtime.node`. |
| `extensions/copilot` | 170 MiB | The built-in Copilot extension. 129 MiB of it is `node_modules/@github`, mostly a second, 107 MiB `runtime.node`. |
| `node` | 121 MiB | Node.js |
| `extensions/mermaid-markdown-features` | 66 MiB | The same webview code three times, tracked in #349688 |
| Everything else | 135 MiB | |

The two `runtime.node` files are different versions on purpose. The built-in extension is pinned to a fixed Copilot CLI version, while the agent host keeps updating ([build/lib/copilot.ts](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/3471806d1de1a84c8984de543239b5a8a4b5a91b/build/lib/copilot.ts#L320-L327), from #327842).

There are smaller duplicates too: `rg` ships three times (in the app, the agent host SDK and the Copilot extension), and so does `tgrep`.

The CLI keeps the last 5 server versions ([`KEEP_LRU`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/3471806d1de1a84c8984de543239b5a8a4b5a91b/cli/src/download_cache.rs#L22)), and stable now ships every week. So one user can have about 5 × 684 MiB ≈ 3.3 GiB in `~/.vscode-server/cli/servers`, and every developer on a shared machine has their own copy. Cleaning up old versions is tracked in #246885, and for Remote-SSH in microsoft/vscode-remote-release#7963.

1. Have the agent host and the built-in Copilot extension share one Copilot runtime. That saves 107 to 157 MiB per installed version.
2. Download the agent host's Copilot SDK the first time the agent host runs on a remote, instead of shipping it in every server. Machines without internet access would still need a way to get it.
3. Ship Mermaid's webview code once (#349688).

Enable Composite Task Multiple Instance Launch

Terminal tasks with `dependsOn` "Child" task(s) should launch new tasks, not attach to current running ones, and respect multiple instances reflected by `instanceLimit` of "Parent" (Composite task) or "Child" task(s).

The offending line seems to be in [terminalTaskSystem.ts#L567](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/3c3f56db86a4034c108ae3642c8a58173d31b1ae/src/vs/workbench/contrib/tasks/browser/terminalTaskSystem.ts#L567). A new dependency is started only if no active instance is found. Otherwise `_getDependencyPromise(activeTask)` is awaited instead, i.e. current running one stays until terminated and a new instance is not launched until that terminates.

1. Dependencies are reused, not duplicated. For each entry in `dependsOn`, VS Code first looks for an already-running instance with the same task label. If it finds one, it waits on that instead of launching a new one. The relevant line is `this._activeTasks[dependencyTask.getMapKey()] ?? this._getInstances(dependencyTask).pop()`.

    > So a second "Parent Task" finds "Child - Task 1" and "Child - Task 2" already running and attaches to them. The reuse check never looks at inputs picked or any other values, so any difference here doesn't seem to make a difference.

2. Top-level runs aren't really capped by `instanceLimit`. In run(), if `instances.length >= instanceLimit`, VS Code doesn't start anything. It returns the existing instance. The limit is not enforced for dependency tasks, because dependencies go through `_executeTask` rather than `run()`.

- "Parent Task" (up to 2 each) has a limit of 4 with policy warn.
- "Child - Task 1" and "Child - Task 2" have a limit of 2 with policy prompt.
- The `instancePolicy` setting only decides what to do once the limit is reached (warn, prompt, and so on), but this isn't even being checked neither at parent or children tasks.

- Launching "Parent Task" again won't start `dependsOn` tasks, i.e. a "Child - Task 1" and "Child - Task 2" tasks. It reuses the running ones, even if you picked a different inputs.
- However, you can -- and currently you end up having to -- run "Child - Task 1" and "Child - Task 2" tasks directly/independently to run additional tasks for the same ones (up to 2 each in this case).

We should be able to run `dependsOn` tasks ("Parent Tasks") were new instances of those children tasks are launched automatically, up to limit if configured with `instanceLimit`, or via property configuration in the task.

Agent Host: secondary window/profile overwrites shared sandbox root config and enables sandbox for other windows

Opening or switching a secondary VS Code window to another profile can silently turn sandbox mode **on** (and overwrite other sandbox settings like `allowLocalNetwork`) for **all** windows and subsequent sessions sharing the same Agent Host — even when the user's Default profile explicitly disables sandboxing (`"chat.agent.sandbox.enabled": false` / `"off"`).

From the user's perspective, sessions in their main window appear to randomly enable sandbox mode and break local MCP servers (`host 127.0.0.1 is local and the sandbox policy does not allow local network access`).

1. **`AgentHostSandboxForwarder` overwrites the host-wide `sandbox` root config on every window connect / configuration change**:
   - In `src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminalContrib/chatAgentTools/browser/agentHostSandboxForwarder.ts`, each workbench window independently pushes `readAgentHostSandboxValues(...)` via `ActionType.RootConfigChanged` (`config: { sandbox: desired }`) whenever a connection comes online or sandbox settings change.
   - `readAgentHostSandboxValues` (`src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminalContrib/chatAgentTools/common/sandboxSettingsReader.ts`) reads the **effective** setting values for that window's profile, including registered/experiment defaults.
   - Because forwarding is last-writer-wins across all connected windows and profiles, any secondary window using a profile that does not explicitly override `chat.agent.sandbox.enabled` (e.g., an empty/test profile when an experiment defaults `chat.agent.sandbox.enabled` to `"on"`, or any profile with different sandbox settings) overwrites the shared Agent Host's `agent-host-config.json` `sandbox` object.
   - That host-wide mutation immediately applies to running sessions and persists for new sessions created in other windows using the Default profile.

2. **Diagnostics gap in `agenthost.log`**:
   - `applySandboxConfig` (`src/vs/platform/agentHost/node/copilot/copilotSessionLauncher.ts`) only logs:
     `Applied SDK sandboxConfig via session.options.update`
   - It does not log the applied values (such as `enabled`, `allowLocalNetwork`) or which client/window dispatched the `RootConfigChanged`, making it very hard to diagnose why sandbox mode flipped unexpectedly.

Setup:
- Default profile explicitly sets `"chat.agent.sandbox.enabled": false` and `"chat.agent.sandbox.network.allowLocalNetwork": true`.
- A secondary profile has no `chat.agent.sandbox.*` settings, so it inherits the experiment default (`enabled: "on"`, `allowLocalNetwork: false`).

Observed sequence in `agenthost.log` and renderer logs:
- `12:58:12.329` — Session `<session-1>` starts with sandbox off; local MCP servers connect normally (`12:58:13.344`).
- `12:58:48.666` — A secondary window switches to the secondary profile (no sandbox overrides).
- `12:58:50.897` — `AgentHostSandboxForwarder` in that secondary window pushes the secondary profile's effective sandbox config (`enabled: "on"`, `allowLocalNetwork: false`) to the shared Agent Host root config:
  `[Copilot:<session-1>] Applied SDK sandboxConfig via session.options.update`
- `12:58:51.900` — Local MCP servers immediately fail:
  `MCP server '<local-mcp>' failed (error): ... host 127.0.0.1 is local and the sandbox policy does not allow local network access`
- `13:05:40.548` — A new session `<session-2>` started in the main window (Default profile) inherits the overwritten host root config, receives sandboxed-environment instructions, and fails local MCP server startup (`13:05:43.254`).
- `13:06:05.602` — Another new session `<session-3>` in the main window also starts with sandbox enabled and fails local MCP startup (`13:06:08.126`).
- `13:06:12.892–13:06:14.124` — Sandbox config is updated back to off before `<session-3>` sends its first turn, leaving `allowLocalNetwork: false` behind in `agent-host-config.json` even though the Default profile has `allowLocalNetwork: true`.

- A secondary window / non-default profile connecting to a shared Agent Host should not silently clobber the sandbox configuration of other windows or sessions (e.g., avoid pushing default/unconfigured profile values over explicit host config, or scope sandbox settings per session/window rather than last-writer-wins global `RootConfigChanged`).
- `agenthost.log` should log the effective sandbox flags (e.g. `enabled`, `allowLocalNetwork`) and the originating client/source when `sandbox` root config changes or `applySandboxConfig` runs.

On Windows, Copilot runs a hook's `powershell` command as `pwsh -nop -nol -c "<command>"`. `pwsh -c` exits with 1 when the last native command fails, so the hook's real exit code is lost. A `userPromptSubmitted` hook that exits with 2 to show a warning is treated as a failed hook.

1. Open the hooks TPI repo (trusted) on Windows and start a new Copilot chat.
2. Send `WARNME reply with ok` (`hook.js` writes `The prompt contains WARNME.` to stderr and exits with 2).

```
$base = Join-Path $env:TEMP ('vscode-git-repro-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N'))
$repo = Join-Path $base 'repo'

    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path (Join-Path $repo $name) | Out-Null
    Set-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $repo "$name\.keep") -Value 'fixture'
    @{ path = "repo/$name" }
[... 10 more lines]
```

Open each workspace in turn, for example `code-insiders --disable-extensions --user-data-dir <fresh-profile-directory> <workspace-file>`. If prompted, trust the generated folder. Run **Git: Show Git Output**. Count `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` calls and compare the timestamps for `Initial repository scan started`, `Opened repository`, and `Initial repository scan completed`.

| Workspace roots | Root probes | Scan start to repository opened | Scan start to first status completed | Initial scan time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 1 | 0.41 s | 0.94 s | 0.42 s |
| 317 | 317 | 5.20 s | 5.90 s | 36.16 s |

Both scans find exactly one repository. The multi-root scan continued probing for about 31 seconds after that repository was opened.

`Model.doInitialScan` still invokes `onDidChangeWorkspaceFolders` with all workspace folders when `git.autoRepositoryDetection` is `false`. The handler queues `openRepository` per folder. `openRepository` is sequenced, and its early existing-repository check matches exact roots, not descendants. The repository returned by `rev-parse --show-toplevel` is deduplicated only after the subprocess call, so descendant folders in this repro still incur separate serialized probes after their common repository has already been opened.

Expected: discover explicitly listed repositories without doing a full Git subprocess lookup for each ordinary descendant of an already resolved repository. Any optimization should still detect genuinely nested repositories, submodules, and worktrees. Alternatively, an opt-in way to pin known repository roots would let users of large multi-root workspaces avoid the redundant probes.

Related: #341763 reports excessive Git calls for a non-Git folder; this repro uses a single valid Git repository and explicitly lists many descendants of it.

Windows: VS Code fails to start with FATAL in install_dir_access.cc due to missing ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES ACL on versioned commit folder

Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes

- VS Code Version: 1.147.0 (commit `8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5`, Electron 43.8.9)
- OS Version: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26300

1. Have VS Code installed on a Windows partition or directory where parent permissions contain specific AppContainer Package SIDs (`S-1-15-2-...`) without an explicit `ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES` (`S-1-15-2-1`) ACE.
2. An update is applied using `win32VersionedUpdate: true`, creating the versioned commit subfolder (e.g., `<install-dir>\8a14f0cc1b`) which inherits those restrictive AppContainer package ACEs.
3. Launch `Code.exe`.
4. The process terminates immediately on startup with exit code `0x80000003` (`STATUS_BREAKPOINT`).

Capturing startup output via Crashpad / console reveals the fatal Electron assertion:

```
[FATAL:electron\shell\browser\win\install_dir_access.cc:52] Sandboxed processes cannot read <install-dir>\8a14f0cc1b: its ACL has an entry for an AppContainer package SID but none for ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES, so Windows denies the sandbox token access. Grant it with: icacls "<install-dir>\8a14f0cc1b" /grant *S-1-15-2-1:(OI)(CI)(RX)
```

Running the suggested `icacls` command on the commit folder immediately resolves the issue and allows VS Code to start normally:
```
icacls "<install-dir>\8a14f0cc1b" /grant "*S-1-15-2-1:(OI)(CI)(RX)" /T
```

- **Upstream Electron PR**: [electron/electron#54382](https://github.com/electron/electron/pull/54382) (refs [electron/electron#51761](https://github.com/electron/electron/issues/51761)). This PR introduced the fail-fast check in `install_dir_access.cc` to abort with actionable remediation rather than crash-looping with `GPU process isn't usable. Goodbye.`
- **Related VS Code Issue**: #335315 tracks startup crashes with `GPU process isn't usable` / `0x80000003` prior to this explicit Electron check.
- **Related VS Code Issue**: #338865 tracks Windows startup and path issues under `win32VersionedUpdate`.

When the updater / installer creates new versioned commit subfolders under `win32VersionedUpdate`, it should ensure `ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES` (`*S-1-15-2-1:(OI)(CI)(RX)`) is explicitly granted or retained so sandboxed child tokens are not blocked by stray AppContainer ACEs on custom install paths.

Agents window: `vscode://agents/new` doesn't open a new session while another session is mid-turn, and there's no way to start one with its prompt sent

Summary

We run a team dashboard that starts coding agents for Jira tickets. With "Open agents in: VS Code Agents window" it opens
`vscode://agents/new?workspace=<file-uri>&prompt=<prompt>` (added in #338225).

When no other session is busy this works: the Agents window shows a New Session in that workspace with the prompt filled in.
When another session is **in the middle of a turn**, the same link brings the running session's chat to the front instead.
The new session's prompt ends up saved as a draft behind **+ New Session**, and nothing tells the user it's there.
They have to notice, click **+ New Session** and press Enter themselves.

- VS Code 1.147.0 (8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5), Windows x64
- Agents window, Copilot agent
- Link opened with the OS shell (`Start-Process "vscode://agents/new?..."`), the same way a browser would open it

1. Open the Agents window and start session A in workspace `C:\Projects\RepoA` with a long-running prompt (a build, for example).
2. While session A is still **Working**, open:
   `vscode://agents/new?workspace=file%3A%2F%2F%2FC%3A%2FProjects%2FRepoB&prompt=Say%20hello`
3. Look at the Agents window.

**Expected:** a New Session composer for `RepoB` is in front with "Say hello" filled in. Session A keeps running in the
background, as it does when you start a new session by hand.

**Actual:** session A's chat comes to the front. No new session composer is shown. Clicking **+ New Session** shows the
composer with `RepoB` and "Say hello" already filled in (the request was kept as a draft).

With session A idle, step 2 opens the New Session composer as expected.

The Agents window is built for running several sessions in parallel. A tool that hands work to it (a dashboard, a CLI, a
ticketing system) has no reliable way to do that while another session is busy. It also has no way to know whether the
new session appeared or became a hidden draft. The user sees nothing happen, and the tool waits for an agent that never
starts.

1. **Bug:** `vscode://agents/new` should always show the new session's composer, whether another session is busy or not,
   without interrupting the running one. If the composer can't be shown, show a notification with
   **Open Draft** (as the Drafts feature already does when you navigate away).
2. **Feature:** an opt-in way to start the session with the prompt **sent**, for trusted callers, for example:
   - a CLI command: `code --agents <folder> --prompt "<text>" [--submit]`, like `code chat` does for Copilot Chat in an editor
     window, or
   - a link parameter such as `&submit=true` that asks for confirmation once per caller or workspace.

   We understand #338225 deliberately leaves the prompt unsent so the user can review it. An opt-in that the user turns on
   (a setting such as `sessions.links.allowSubmit`) would keep that the default.
3. **Nice to have:** a way for the caller to learn which session it created (an id in the CLI's output, for example), so a
   tool can follow that session instead of guessing.

We copy the prompt to the clipboard and show a note: "click + New Session; your prompt is waiting there as a draft; press Enter".

Pasting text copied from another application occasionally **permanently freezes the VSCode window**: the UI stops updating entirely (static frame, no cursor blink), never recovers, and the only remedy is closing and reopening the window. Other applications (e.g. Google Chrome) keep pasting fine at the same moment.

In the affected setups this happens a few times per week on X11, typically when pasting content that was synced over RDP (gnome-remote-desktop clipboard integration on the host), but the underlying defect does not involve RDP at all — see the reproducer below, which only uses `xclip`.

- VSCode 1.147.0 (also observed on 1.146.0), Electron 43.8.6
- Ubuntu 24.04.5, X11 session (Xorg), kernel 6.8, x64

Frozen renderer (gdb, three real-world occurrences + one synthetic, all identical):

```
#0  __futex_abstimed_wait_common64 (... abstime=0x0 ...)     <- no timeout
#3  __pthread_cond_wait_common (abstime=0x0)
#4  ___pthread_cond_wait
#5  0x… in ??? ()          <- code+0x1e2bfd4, same offset every time
```

- Renderer main thread parked forever in an unbounded condvar wait — a synchronous wait for the browser-side clipboard read result triggered by paste handling.
- 0 % CPU, zero voluntary context switches afterwards, no further log output.
- The browser (main) process is completely healthy (all threads in normal idle waits).
- The X11 selection owner at the time of the freezes answers every request correctly within milliseconds — verified with a raw `XConvertSelection` probe for both advertised and unadvertised targets, including proper `property=None` refusals (ICCCM-compliant).

Mechanism: on X11 a clipboard read requires a round trip (`SelectionRequest` → `SelectionNotify`). If the selection owner exits or hands over ownership **while the content request is in flight**, the reply is never delivered. The X11 clipboard implementation in use here has **no timeout and no cancellation of in-flight selection requests on ownership change**, so the pending read never completes and the renderer-side synchronous clipboard read blocks its main thread forever → frozen window.

This is exactly the situation that occurs in real life when a clipboard backend restarts (RDP daemon, clipboard manager), a remote session drops, or the user pastes within milliseconds of copying (ownership handoff still in progress).

Chrome survives the identical situation because its paste path reads the clipboard asynchronously — the read may never complete, but the UI thread never blocks.

Model routers

A model router lets you decide which model a chat uses for which kind of work. You write the routes once, such as a small model for quick questions and a large one for hard problems, and pick the router in the model picker like any other model. For each chat, the router reads your request, picks the route that fits, and says which one it picked.

Model routers are a preview for Copilot sessions in the Agent Host, behind the setting `chat.copilot.modelRouter.enabled`. This issue tracks the feature: what works today and what is planned.

A router is a YAML file, `<name>.model-router.yaml`, in `~/.agents/model-routers/`.

**Writing a router**
- Routers are files in `~/.agents/model-routers/` (or `~/.copilot/model-routers/`). A new or changed file is picked up within a few seconds, without a reload.
- The built-in `/model-router` skill writes, checks and cleans up routers, and its `check_model_router` tool reports problems and lists the models your account can use.
- A router with a mistake stays in the model picker with a warning and the error, and a chat that uses it keeps its current model.

**Routes**
- A router has 2 to 10 routes. Each has a `when` that says which requests it is for, and can have `examples`. The first route is used when the router can't tell.
- `model` is a model id, a model family such as `opus` (the newest model of that family you can use), or a list that is tried in order.
- `effort` can be set on a route. Without it, the router chooses an effort for each request, or leaves the model's default when the router says `effort: off`.
- `context-size: long` runs a route's model on its larger context window, where the model has one.
- Routes can have a `name`. Named routes can share a model, for example the same model at two effort levels.

**How a chat is routed**
- By default a router picks a route from a chat's first message and keeps it for that chat.
- With `switching: auto`, later messages are routed too, and the chat moves to another route when the work clearly changes. Replies such as "ok, continue" stay on the current route.
- Besides the message, the decision knows what is attached, whether the chat is in Plan mode, the custom agent you chose, and the workspace it is in.
- Choosing a custom agent that names its own model puts the chat on that model. Picking the router after it routes the chat again.

**Guidance**
- A route's `guidance` is given to the chat's main agent. It says how you want that kind of work done: the steps to take, and the skills and custom agents to use. When a chat moves to another route, it gets that route's guidance.
- A router with a single route is allowed when the route has guidance: one way of working, written down once.
- A router's own top-level `guidance` is for the routing decision only.

**In the UI**
- The model picker has a Routers tab. A router's Details show its routes with their model, effort and context size, whether it switches routes, and a link to its file.
- The chat shows a routing line when a route is picked or changed, such as "Daily Driver picked its quick route on *model* · Low effort", and a notice when a router could not be used.

Extension auto-update keeps re-downloading VSIX files indefinitely when the disk is full (ENOSPC)

Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: N/A (the issue is in the extension auto-update mechanism itself)

- VS Code Version: 1.145.2 (c4453f8ea430795f941c1b2ff6c9321135a74a02), x64, snap (`latest/stable`)
- OS Version: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, Linux 7.0.0-42-generic

When the disk is full, extension auto-update fails with `ENOSPC` while writing the downloaded VSIX to `CachedExtensionVSIXs`. VS Code then retries, and starts the whole update again at the next update cycle, with no limit. Every attempt downloads the VSIX again. Nothing tells the user that updates are failing or that the disk is full.

Over about two days, the shared process log records **136 `ENOSPC` errors** for two extensions with large platform-specific VSIX packages (`anthropic.claude-code` and `openai.chatgpt`, roughly 100–180 MB each):

| | `anthropic.claude-code` | `openai.chatgpt` |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed downloading vsix … Retry again...` | 37 | 36 |
| `Error while installing the extension` | 18 | 19 |

| Day | `ENOSPC` log lines |
|---|---|
| Day 1 | 55 |
| Day 2 | 62 |
| Day 3 (partial, until the disk was cleaned) | 19 |

While the loop was running, I measured the VS Code process receiving about **2.8 MB/s** from the Marketplace CDN, with the machine otherwise idle. On a metered or limited connection, this silently uses several GB of data.

1. Have at least one extension with a pending update (a large platform-specific VSIX makes the effect more visible).
2. Fill the disk until less free space is left than the size of the VSIX.
3. Keep VS Code open with extension auto-update enabled (the default).
4. Watch `sharedprocess.log` and the network traffic of the VS Code process.

Each update cycle downloads the VSIX up to 3 times. The download fails on write, and the install errors out. The next auto-update check then starts over. Typical sequence (paths shortened):

```
14:15:16.251 [info]    Installing extension: anthropic.claude-code {... "operation":3 ...}
14:15:16.302 [info]    Installing extension: openai.chatgpt {... "operation":3 ...}
14:15:51.666 [warning] Failed downloading vsix. Unable to write file '~/.config/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/.424001bb-…' (Unknown (FileSystemError): Error: ENOSPC: no space left on device, write). Retry again... anthropic.claude-code
14:15:51.670 [warning] Failed downloading vsix. Unable to write file '~/.config/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/.f4cf3ff3-…' (… ENOSPC …). Retry again... openai.chatgpt
14:16:35.689 [warning] Failed downloading vsix. … ENOSPC … Retry again... anthropic.claude-code
14:16:35.691 [warning] Failed downloading vsix. … ENOSPC … Retry again... openai.chatgpt
14:17:53.396 [error]   Error while installing the extension openai.chatgpt Unable to write file '~/.config/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/.27c84aea-…' (… ENOSPC …)
14:19:38.594 [error]   Error while installing the extension anthropic.claude-code Unable to write file '~/.config/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/.ed3a7399-…' (… ENOSPC …)
15:28:44.525 [info]    Installing extension: anthropic.claude-code {... "operation":3 ...}

```

This continued until I freed disk space manually. The next update attempt after the cleanup (`openai.chatgpt`) succeeded right away.

- Treat `ENOSPC` as a non-transient error: do not retry the download right away, since the next attempt will fail in the same way.
- Back off between update cycles that fail (or skip the extension until free space changes), instead of downloading the same VSIX again on every check.
- Tell the user, once, that extension updates are failing because the disk is full.

- #343873: abandoned `.<UUID>` temporary files in `CachedExtensionVSIXs` are never cleaned up. Here, each failed attempt left such a file behind (about 420 MB of partial downloads in total), which took up more of the already full disk and kept the loop going.

Mermaid extension ships 35 MB of duplicate copies of its webview code

The built-in `mermaid-markdown-features` extension takes 65 MB, and 35.4 MB of that is byte-identical copies of the same files. Building its webviews in one esbuild run instead of four makes it 18.5 MB.

[`esbuild.webview.mts`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/17befd82f733a3b65274e6d1206f616664f9e0df/extensions/mermaid-markdown-features/esbuild.webview.mts#L38-L92) builds the webviews in four separate esbuild runs, each into its own folder:

| Output folder | Size |
|---|---|
| `markdown-preview-out` | 18.2 MB |
| `notebook-out` | 18.2 MB |
| `markdown-editor-out` | 18.2 MB |
| `chat-webview-out` | 10.2 MB |

The Markdown preview, notebook and Markdown editor builds use `splitting: true`. But because each is its own esbuild run, each one writes its own copy of every chunk. 204 files are duplicated. The largest:

| File | Size | Copies |
|---|---|---|
| `logos-*.js` (icon pack) | 7.0 MB | 3 |
| `mdi-*.js` (icon pack) | 3.0 MB | 3 |
| `zenuml-definition-*.js` | 1.6 MB | 3 |
| `chunk-*.js` | 1.5 MB | 3 |
| `elk-*.js` | 1.4 MB | 3 |

The chat build doesn't use splitting, so its `index.js` and `index-editor.js` are two 5.3 MB bundles that each contain all of Mermaid and are nearly identical.

To see it:

```
cd extensions/mermaid-markdown-features
du -sh *-out
shasum */logos-*.js
```

- **Disk:** 65 MB in every install.
- **Download:** the `.zip` and `.tar.gz` packages use deflate, which only finds repeats within 32 KB, so the copies are not compressed away. Compressed file by file, the extension is 19.8 MB, and 10.8 MB of that is the copies.
- **VS Code Server:** the extension has a `main` and no `extensionKind`, so the [server build](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/17befd82f733a3b65274e6d1206f616664f9e0df/build/gulpfile.reh.ts#L263-L288) includes it. The Insiders server for macOS arm64 (commit 0d15d4d) contains all 64.9 MB of it.

Building all six entry points in one esbuild run, with `splitting: true` and one output folder, produces **18.5 MB** (5.7 MB compressed file by file) with no duplicates. Combining only the three Mermaid builds and leaving the chat build as it is gives about 28.5 MB.

A change along those lines needs to:

- update the places that reference the four output folders;
- check that the chat webview can load chunks, since today it gets everything in one file.

The two icon packs, 10 MB of the 18.5 MB, are already loaded only when a diagram uses them ([`iconPackConfig.ts`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/17befd82f733a3b65274e6d1206f616664f9e0df/extensions/mermaid-markdown-features/preview-src/shared/iconPackConfig.ts)).

* Failing to identify `old_text` as a required parameter.
* Failing to satisfy the strict formatting and exact-match requirements of the `old_text` string parameter (e.g, quote escaping, exact whitespace matching).

Currently, these models fail consistently even at higher precisions (`Q8_0` or `BF16`). Because this behavior reproduces across both native GitHub Copilot features and third-party extension host harnesses (e.g., Cline, Claude Code, Kilo), extension-specific bugs have been ruled out.

To make the editor tool call more resilient for smaller context/parameter models, consider one or more of the following adjustments:
1. **Flexible Whitespace Matching:** Introduce a lenient whitespace matching mode for `old_text` that normalizes minor indentation or line-ending discrepancies that otherwise behave identically in the editor.
2. **Line-Based Replacement Schema:** Support an alternative, structured OpenAI-compatible schema for edits—such as an array of objects specifying line ranges paired with a `new_text` string—rather than relying solely on exact string matching via `old_text`.
3. **Relaxed String Escaping:** Make string parsing more forgiving for models that struggle with heavy quote escaping across multi-line code blocks.

Improving tool-call resilience for sub-8B models directly supports developers working on constrained local hardware, budget-conscious workflows without cloud API access, and enterprise/privacy-strict environments where cloud-based LLMs are prohibited.
